article.title: Why Buying More Categories Can Signal a Deeper Customer Relationship
article.why: Practical analytical English for data-driven decisions.

paragraphs.en: Category breadth can reveal whether a customer is using a retailer for more needs, even when total spending is stable. A shopper who buys only vegetables and then begins buying prepared food, household goods, and health products may be building a broader relationship. However, one promotional purchase should not automatically be treated as deeper loyalty. Analysts should distinguish repeated category adoption from temporary trial. They can track the number of categories purchased, the months in which each category appears, and whether new categories remain active after a campaign ends. Basket size and visit frequency add context. If category breadth rises while spending and visits collapse, the interpretation may be weak. If breadth rises together with repeat visits and retention, the signal is stronger. Category definitions also matter. Very narrow product classifications can make breadth look artificially high, while categories that are too broad can hide meaningful expansion. A stable hierarchy is therefore important for year-over-year comparison. Analysts should also separate customer need from marketing influence. A household event, season, or life-stage change may naturally expand purchases. Experiments can test whether recommendations or benefits cause additional cross-category adoption. The practical lesson is that category breadth is not simply another count. It can describe the depth of a customer relationship when it is persistent, economically meaningful, and measured with consistent definitions. A useful report should show both breadth and repeat behavior so that managers can see whether customers are truly adding the retailer to more parts of their routine.  Analysts should document the population, observation window, assumptions, and operational definition. This makes the conclusion reproducible and helps separate a headline result from the mechanism that produced it.
